title: Stab
intro: Stab wants recognition without surrendering access. The speaker makes an entrance, declares himself a legend and insists on his reality, but asks to be treated as though he never appeared. That tension becomes explicit when he withholds his story because success would make it useful to other people. Half a yuan is enough for style; the bigger risk is allowing someone else to own the meaning of that style. Time becomes the imagined witness who can eventually recognise him without exploiting him now.
reading: Visibility desired, possession resisted; privacy is a consequence of anticipated success rather than simple modesty.

revisions.editorial-18-never-here: The next lines announce an entrance, so the request for erasure is not straightforward reluctance to perform. He wants to choose the terms on which his presence is available. Later, he says his story could be used against or for other people's purposes at his brightest moment. That gives the hook a concrete conflict: being seen helps make a legend, but being fully accessible makes a person exploitable.
revisions.18-river: The proverb ordinarily warns that repeated proximity to danger eventually has consequences. He grants himself an exemption, walking beside the water without getting wet. But the later refusal to tell his story is a precaution, which means the verse is less carefree than the boast claims. He performs immunity while actively managing exposure. The protection is work even when the persona makes it look effortless.
revisions.editorial-18-half-yuan: The tiny amount in his pocket breaks the expected connection between wealth and visible confidence. This is a claim to style that does not require receipts. It also makes the later fear of exploitation more specific: someone with little money can still possess a story or image others want to use. His value in the song is not identical with what he currently owns.
revisions.editorial-18-time-knows: He appoints time as the witness after declining to give the current audience all the evidence. That postpones recognition rather than abandoning it. 'I know I am real' has not eliminated the wish for somebody else to know it too. The repeated promise lets him imagine eventual vindication while preserving present privacy, then leads back into the legend who both appears and disappears.
